recipe: Import useRef, declare a ref with useRef(null), pass it as the ref attribute to the target JSX element, and access the DOM node through ref.current after React mounts it.
trigger_condition: You need to interact with a DOM node managed by React, such as focusing an input, scrolling to an element, or measuring its size.
evidence: The `useRef` Hook returns an object with a single property called `current`. Initially, `myRef.current` will be `null`. When React creates a DOM node for this `<div>`, React will put a reference to this node into `myRef.current`.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Do not call useRef inside a map() call, loop, or condition; instead, use a ref callback that stores each node in a Map or array keyed by item ID.
trigger_condition: You need a ref for every item in a dynamically rendered list whose length is not known at compile time.
evidence: This is because **Hooks must only be called at the top-level of your component.** You can't call `useRef` in a loop, in a condition, or inside a `map()` call.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Pass a function to the ref attribute; inside it, store the DOM node in a shared Map on mount and return a cleanup function that removes it from the Map on unmount.
trigger_condition: You need to maintain a collection of refs for a variable number of list items and access any individual node by its identifier.
evidence: Another solution is to **pass a function to the `ref` attribute.** This is called a [`ref` callback.](/reference/react-dom/components/common#ref-callback) React will call your ref callback with the DOM node when it's time to set the ref, and call the cleanup function returned from the callback when it's time to clear it.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Create a ref in the parent component, pass it to the child as a prop, and have the child forward it to the underlying DOM element so the parent can read the node from ref.current.
trigger_condition: You need to access a DOM node that lives inside a child component from the parent.
evidence: You can pass refs from parent component to child components [just like any other prop](/learn/passing-props-to-a-component).
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Use useImperativeHandle to expose only a curated subset of methods (e.g., just focus) to the parent instead of the full DOM node API.
trigger_condition: You want to restrict what a parent component can do with a child's DOM node to a small, well-defined interface.
evidence: In uncommon cases, you may want to restrict the exposed functionality. You can do that with [`useImperativeHandle`](/reference/react/useImperativeHandle):
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Write ref callbacks to be idempotent (safe to call twice) because React Strict Mode will invoke them twice in development.
trigger_condition: You are using ref callbacks and have React Strict Mode enabled in your development environment.
evidence: When Strict Mode is enabled, ref callbacks will run twice in development.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Access refs from event handlers rather than during rendering, since DOM nodes are not yet available or updated during the render phase.
trigger_condition: You need to read or write a ref that holds a DOM node.
evidence: Usually, you will access refs from event handlers.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Avoid manually modifying, adding children to, or removing children from DOM nodes that React manages, as this can lead to inconsistent visual results or crashes.
trigger_condition: You are considering using a DOM API like remove() or appendChild() on an element rendered by React.
evidence: Avoid changing DOM nodes managed by React.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Use refs primarily for non-destructive actions like focusing, scrolling, or measuring DOM elements rather than for replacing React's declarative updates.
trigger_condition: You are deciding whether to use a ref or a React state/prop to accomplish a task.
evidence: Usually, you will use refs for non-destructive actions like focusing, scrolling, or measuring DOM elements.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Wrap your state update in `flushSync` before calling `scrollIntoView()` on a ref, so React commits the DOM change first and the ref points to the correct node.
trigger_condition: You need to scroll a DOM element after changing React state that determines which element is active.
evidence: the `flushSync` call is necessary to force React to update the DOM before the scroll. Otherwise, `selectedRef.current` would always point at the previously selected item.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Attach a single ref conditionally (e.g., `ref={index === i ? selectedRef : null}`) so it only binds to the currently active element in a list.
trigger_condition: You only need a ref to the currently selected or active element rather than to every element in a rendered list.
evidence: You don't need to have a ref to every image for this exercise. It should be enough to have a ref to the currently active image, or to the list itself.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

recipe: Pass `ref` as a prop to a custom component and forward it to the underlying DOM element so the parent can call methods like `focus()` on it.
trigger_condition: A child component wraps a DOM element and the parent needs to call browser methods (e.g., `focus()`) on that element.
evidence: You'll need to pass `ref` as a prop to opt into exposing a DOM node from your own component like `SearchInput`.
source_name: react.dev learn: Manipulating the DOM with Refs

trigger_condition: You need to bring a specific element into view within a horizontally scrollable gallery or list.
